sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: です links a subject to a predicate noun or na-adjective as the polite form of だ. It appears at the end of polite sentences and is the single most characteristic word of polite Japanese speech. です does not conjugate like a verb; tense and negation are expressed through its auxiliary forms (でした, ではありません, ではありませんでした).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun or na-adjective + です

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Often follows い-adjectives (e.g., 高いです) as a politeness marker, even though it is not formally copular in that use.
The plain-form equivalent is だ. In feminine plain speech だ is often dropped entirely.

examples.furi: これは<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>です。
田中さんは<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>です。
<ruby>今日<rt>こんにち</rt></ruby>は<ruby>月曜日<rt>げつようび</rt></ruby>です。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: だ is the plain-form copula, used in casual speech, writing, and when attaching copular predicates to grammatical constructions that require the plain form (e.g., before と in quotation or before から in giving reasons). In feminine and neutral speech だ is often dropped at the end of standalone sentences.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun or na-adjective + だ

sections.label: Register
sections.html: casual

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Dropping だ at the end of a sentence is common in casual female speech and gender-neutral speech.
Before certain particles and grammatical markers, だ is required even where it would otherwise be dropped.

examples.furi: これは<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う。
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みだ。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: でした is the polite past form of the copula, used to state that something was (in the past) something. It is the past tense counterpart of です and applies to nouns and na-adjectives.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun or na-adjective + でした

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html: For い-adjectives, do not use でした — use かったです instead (e.g., 高かったです, not 高いでした).

examples.furi: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>日曜日<rt>にちようび</rt></ruby>でした。
<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>元気<rt>げんき</rt></ruby>でした。

examples.jp: あの映画はとても有名でした。
examples.furi: あの<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>はとても<ruby>有名<rt>ゆうめい</rt></ruby>でした。

related: い-adjective stem + かった(です)

meaning: is not / am not / are not (polite negative copula)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: ではありません is the polite negative form of the copula, used to deny that something is something. The contracted じゃありません is equally polite and more common in casual polite speech; じゃないです is another common variant. The plain-form equivalent is ではない or じゃない.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun or na-adjective + ではありません

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
じゃありません is a colloquial contraction that is still polite; both are acceptable in polite speech.
The past negative form is ではありませんでした (or じゃありませんでした).

examples.jp: これはペンではありません。
examples.furi: これはペンではありません。

examples.jp: 彼は日本人じゃありません。
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>人じゃありません。

examples.jp: 今日は月曜日ではありません。
examples.furi: <ruby>今日<rt>こんにち</rt></ruby>は<ruby>月曜日<rt>げつようび</rt></ruby>ではありません。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: ます is the polite non-past verb ending. Every Japanese verb can be conjugated into its ます form by attaching the ます ending to the verb stem. The ます form is used in polite speech with strangers, customers, teachers, and in business contexts. It expresses both present and future tense depending on context.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Ichidan verb: drop る, add ます (食べる → 食べます). Godan verb: change the final う-row kana to the corresponding い-row kana, then add ます (行く → 行きます, 話す → 話します).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Irregular verbs: する → します, くる → きます.
The ます form covers both present and future time; context distinguishes them.
The plain-form equivalent is the dictionary form (食べる, 行く).

examples.jp: 毎朝、コーヒーを飲みます。
examples.furi: <ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby>、コーヒーを<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みます。

examples.en: I will go to Tokyo tomorrow.
examples.furi: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語を<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>します。

related: Verb stem + ませんでした

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: ました is the polite past form of a verb, expressing that an action happened or was completed in the past. It replaces ます on the verb stem.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Same verb stem as ます, then + ました instead of ます

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html: Used for both single past events and completed actions.

examples.furi: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ました。

examples.jp: 朝ごはんを食べました。
examples.furi: <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べました。

examples.jp: 友だちに手紙を書きました。
examples.en: I wrote a letter to my friend.
examples.furi: <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちに<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>しょ</rt></ruby>きました。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: ません is the polite negative non-past form of a verb. It expresses that an action is not being done or will not be done.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Same verb stem as ます, then + ません instead of ます

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html: Covers both 'do not' and 'will not'.

examples.furi: お<ruby>酒<rt>さけ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みません。

examples.jp: 今日は学校へ行きません。
examples.en: I'm not going to school today.
examples.furi: <ruby>今日<rt>こんにち</rt></ruby>は<ruby>学校<rt>がっこう</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きません。

examples.jp: 朝ごはんを食べません。
examples.furi: <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べません。

related: Verb stem + ませんでした

point: Verb stem + ませんでした

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: ませんでした is the polite past negative form of a verb. It expresses that an action did not happen.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Same verb stem as ます, then + ませんでした instead of ます

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Form by replacing ます with ませんでした: 食べます → 食べませんでした, 行きます → 行きませんでした.
For い-adjective past negative, use くなかったです (e.g., 高くなかったです), not ませんでした. The ませんでした form is only for verbs.

examples.jp: 昨日、宿題をしませんでした。
examples.en: I didn't do my homework yesterday.
examples.furi: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>をしませんでした。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>らい</rt></ruby>ませんでした。

examples.jp: 先週、一度も泳ぎませんでした。
examples.en: I didn't swim even once last week.
examples.furi: <ruby>先週<rt>せんしゅう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby>も<ruby>泳<rt>およ</rt></ruby>ぎませんでした。

meaning: marks the topic of a sentence (pronounced 'wa')

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: は marks the topic of a sentence — the thing the sentence is about. The topic is typically already known to both speaker and listener, in contrast to が which introduces new or focal information. は is always written with the hiragana は but is pronounced 'wa' as a particle. Understanding the は/が distinction is one of the most important and most difficult points for new learners.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + は

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Always written with the kana は, not わ, when used as a topic particle.
In questions and answers, newly introduced subjects often take が, and once established as the topic they shift to は.
Multiple topics can be marked in a single sentence for contrastive emphasis (私は日本語は分かります — 'as for me, Japanese I understand').

examples.furi: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>です。

examples.jp: 今日は天気がいいですね。
examples.en: The weather is nice today, isn't it.
examples.furi: <ruby>今日<rt>こんにち</rt></ruby>は<ruby>天気<rt>てんき</rt></ruby>がいいですね。
この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いです。

meaning: marks the grammatical subject; introduces new information

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: が marks the grammatical subject of a sentence and often introduces new or focal information — the answer to a question word like 'who?' or 'what?'. It contrasts with は (the topic marker) in that は presupposes the subject is already known, while が asserts it as new or contrasts it with alternatives. が is also required with certain stative predicates (好き, 欲しい, 分かる, できる, etc.).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + が

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Use が with stative predicates: 日本語が分かります, コーヒーが好きです.
In response to a question word subject, answer with が: Who came? — 田中さんが来ました.
が can also mean 'but' as a conjunction in mid-sentence — that is a different usage.

examples.furi: <ruby>誰<rt>だれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>来<rt>らい</rt></ruby>ましたか。
田中さんが<ruby>来<rt>らい</rt></ruby>ました。
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語が<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かります。

meaning: marks the direct object of a transitive verb

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: を marks the direct object of a transitive verb — the thing that the action is done to. Despite being written with the kana を, it is pronounced the same as お. を is used only as this particle in modern Japanese; the kana appears for no other purpose.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + を + transitive verb

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Always written with を, pronounced 'o'.
Also marks the path of motion verbs: 公園を散歩する ('walk through the park'), 道を渡る ('cross the road').

examples.furi: <ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みます。
<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>を<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みます。
<ruby>公園<rt>こうえん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>散歩<rt>さんぽ</rt></ruby>しました。

meaning: marks target, destination, location of existence, or time

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: に has several related uses: (1) target of an action (手紙を友だちに書く), (2) destination of motion (東京に行く), (3) location where something exists with ある/いる (机の上に本がある), (4) a specific point in time (三時に会いましょう). It is one of the most commonly used particles and the correct use requires seeing many examples.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + に

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
For motion destination, に and へ are often interchangeable, though に is more common.
For location of action (where the action takes place), use で, not に. に marks where something IS (with ある/いる); で marks where something HAPPENS.

examples.jp: 友だちに手紙を書きます。
examples.en: I write a letter to my friend.
examples.furi: <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちに<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>しょ</rt></ruby>きます。
<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。

examples.jp: 机の上に本があります。
examples.en: There is a book on the desk.
examples.furi: <ruby>机<rt>つくえ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>があります。

examples.en: I wake up at seven o'clock.
examples.furi: 七時に<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きます。

meaning: marks the means, tool, or location of an action

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: で has two main uses: (1) the means or tool by which something is done (バスで行く — 'go by bus'; 日本語で話す — 'speak in Japanese'), and (2) the location where an action takes place (図書館で勉強する — 'study at the library'). Contrast with に for location of EXISTENCE rather than action.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + で + action verb

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Location: use で for where an action happens, に for where something exists.
Also used to mark quantity/limit (五千円で買う — 'buy for 5,000 yen').

examples.jp: バスで学校に行きます。
examples.en: I go to school by bus.
examples.furi: バスで<ruby>学校<rt>がっこう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。
<ruby>図書館<rt>としょかん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>します。

examples.jp: 日本語で話してください。
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語で<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>してください。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: と connects two or more nouns in an exhaustive 'X and Y' listing, where the list is complete. It is also used to mark the person or thing you are doing something WITH (友だちと映画を見る — 'watch a movie with a friend'). A third use, quotation, is a different grammar point.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + と + Noun (listing); Person + と + verb (accompaniment)

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
For non-exhaustive listing ('X, Y, and such'), use や instead of と.
For the quotation use (saying/thinking/calling), see to-iu.

examples.jp: パンと牛乳を買いました。
examples.furi: パンと<ruby>牛乳<rt>ぎゅうにゅう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>いました。

examples.jp: 友だちと食事をしました。
examples.en: I had a meal with a friend.
examples.furi: <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちと<ruby>食事<rt>しょくじ</rt></ruby>をしました。

examples.jp: 母と電話で話しました。
examples.en: I talked with my mother on the phone.
examples.furi: <ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>と<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>しました。

meaning: marks possession; modifies a noun with another noun

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: の is the most versatile particle for linking nouns. It marks possession (私の本 — 'my book'), and more generally it connects two nouns where the first modifies or describes the second (日本語の先生 — 'Japanese language teacher', 日本の車 — 'Japanese car', 木のテーブル — 'wooden table'). It is also used to nominalize verbs, which is a separate N4 topic.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun1 + の + Noun2 (Noun2 is the head; Noun1 modifies it)

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Multiple の can chain: 私の友だちの車 — 'my friend's car'.
The nominalizing use (e.g., 食べるのが好き) appears later at higher levels.

examples.furi: これは<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>の<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>です。

examples.jp: 彼は日本語の先生です。
examples.en: He is a Japanese language teacher.
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語の<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>です。

examples.jp: あの赤い車は田中さんのです。
examples.en: That red car is Mr. Tanaka's.
examples.furi: あの<ruby>赤<rt>あか</rt></ruby>い<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby>は田中さんのです。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: へ marks direction of movement — 'to' a place. It is very similar to に used for motion destination; in most contexts the two are interchangeable, with へ emphasizing the direction of movement slightly more than arrival. へ is always written with the kana へ but pronounced 'e' when used as a particle.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun (place) + へ + motion verb

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Written へ, pronounced 'e' as a particle.
Overlapping meaning with に for motion destination; に is more common in casual usage.

examples.furi: <ruby>学校<rt>がっこう</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>しました。

examples.jp: 友だちの家へ遊びに行きます。
examples.en: I'm going to my friend's house to hang out.
examples.furi: <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちの<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>びに<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: から marks the starting point of an action or movement — 'from' a place or 'since/from' a time. It is often paired with まで to express a range ('from X until Y'). A separate use of から is 'because' (also N5 — see kara-cause).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun (place or time) + から

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Place: 家から学校まで ('from home to school').
Time: 九時から五時まで ('from 9 to 5').
The 'because' meaning attaches to verbs/adjectives/sentences, not nouns, and is also N5 (see kara-cause).

examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>から<ruby>来<rt>らい</rt></ruby>ました。

examples.jp: 九時から授業が始まります。
examples.furi: 九時から<ruby>授業<rt>じゅぎょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>まります。

examples.jp: この手紙は友だちからです。
examples.en: This letter is from a friend.
examples.furi: この<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちからです。

related: Plain or polite form + から

meaning: marks the endpoint: until / as far as

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: まで marks the endpoint of movement or action — 'until' a time or 'as far as' a place. Commonly paired with から to express a range. まで implies the full extent up to and including the endpoint.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun (place or time) + まで

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Often paired with から: X から Y まで.
Contrast with までに ('by [deadline]') — see N4.

examples.furi: <ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>まで<ruby>歩<rt>ほ</rt></ruby>きます。

examples.jp: 夜十時まで働きました。
examples.en: I worked until ten at night.
examples.furi: 夜十時まで<ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>きました。

examples.jp: 月曜日から金曜日まで学校があります。
examples.en: I have school from Monday to Friday.
examples.furi: <ruby>月曜日<rt>げつようび</rt></ruby>から<ruby>金曜日<rt>きんようび</rt></ruby>まで<ruby>学校<rt>がっこう</rt></ruby>があります。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: も marks addition — 'also' or 'too'. It replaces は or を (and sometimes が) in the position it would otherwise occupy. In negative sentences it translates as 'either' or '(not) any'.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + も (replacing は, が, or を)

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
も replaces the particle it would normally take: 私もコーヒーを飲みます, not 私はもコーヒーを飲みます.
With quantity, 何もない ('nothing'), 誰もいない ('no one is here').

examples.furi: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>も<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>です。

examples.jp: 彼もコーヒーを飲みます。
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>もコーヒーを<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みます。
この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>も<ruby>面白<rt>おもしろ</rt></ruby>いです。

meaning: marks a sentence as a question

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: か at the end of a sentence turns it into a question in polite speech. In casual speech the か is often dropped and rising intonation alone signals a question. か also appears embedded in sentences to mark indirect questions (私は知りません + 何時に来るか → 何時に来るか知りません, 'I don't know when he's coming').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Statement in polite form + か

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
In casual speech か is typically replaced by rising intonation alone.
Embedded questions use か at the end of the embedded clause.

examples.furi: これは<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby>ですか。

examples.jp: 日本語が分かりますか。
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語が<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりますか。

examples.en: Are you coming to school tomorrow?
examples.furi: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、<ruby>学校<rt>がっこう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>らい</rt></ruby>ますか。

meaning: right? / isn't it? (seeking agreement or confirming shared knowledge)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: ね at the end of a sentence signals that the speaker assumes the listener shares their view or knowledge — 'right?', 'isn't it?'. It softens a statement and invites the listener's agreement. It is a sentence-final particle and can appear after both plain and polite forms.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Sentence (any form) + ね

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Extended or emphatic pronunciation ねー, ねぇ are common.
ね differs from よ: ね seeks shared agreement; よ asserts or informs.

examples.jp: 今日はいい天気ですね。
examples.en: The weather is nice today, isn't it.
examples.furi: <ruby>今日<rt>こんにち</rt></ruby>はいい<ruby>天気<rt>てんき</rt></ruby>ですね。

examples.jp: あの映画は面白かったですね。
examples.en: That movie was interesting, wasn't it.
examples.furi: あの<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>は<ruby>面白<rt>おもしろ</rt></ruby>かったですね。

examples.jp: この料理はおいしいですね。
examples.en: This food is delicious, isn't it.
examples.furi: この<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>はおいしいですね。

meaning: I'm telling you / emphasis; informs the listener of new information

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: よ at the end of a sentence emphasizes the statement and informs the listener of something the speaker believes the listener does not already know. It can feel assertive or inviting depending on tone. よ contrasts with ね: よ asserts; ね seeks agreement.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Sentence (any form) + よ

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Overuse of よ can sound pushy or condescending.
よね combines the two: asserting while seeking confirmation ('that's right, isn't it?').

examples.en: That store is cheap, you know.

meaning: this / that / that over there / which (pronominal demonstratives)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: これ refers to something near the speaker, それ to something near the listener (or already mentioned), あれ to something far from both, and どれ asks 'which one?'. This three-way distance distinction (ko-so-a-do system) pervades Japanese demonstratives. These forms stand alone as pronouns; the parallel attributive forms この/その/あの/どの precede a noun.

sections.html: これ/それ/あれ/どれ + verb/copula

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
これ is a full pronoun; use この before a noun ('this book' = この本, not これ本).
どれ is used when choosing from 3+ options; for 2 options, どちら is more appropriate.

Same ko-so-a-do distance distinction as these pronouns.

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The ko-so-a-do demonstratives for place: ここ is 'here' (where the speaker is), そこ is 'there' (where the listener is or already mentioned), あそこ is 'over there' (far from both), and どこ asks 'where?'. Note the irregular あそこ (not ああこ).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: ここ/そこ/あそこ/どこ + copula or particle

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
あそこ is irregular: it's あそこ, not 'あこ' or 'ああこ'.
The more polite and abstract directional forms こちら/そちら/あちら/どちら are taught as a separate point.

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: あります is the polite existential verb for inanimate things (including plants, abstract concepts, and events). It is paired with います for animate things (people and animals). The thing that exists is marked with が; the place of existence is marked with に.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Place + に + Thing + が + あります

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
For animate things (people, animals), use います instead.
The thing that exists takes が, not は. If emphasizing the place as the topic, the place itself takes は: テーブルの上には何がありますか.
ない is the plain negative (ありません in polite form); あった is the plain past; なかった is plain past negative.

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: います is the polite existential verb for animate beings — people and animals. It parallels あります exactly in structure but is used exclusively for animates. The distinction is strict: using あります for a person is grammatically wrong and will sound jarring.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Place + に + Animate + が + います

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Use for people, pets, wild animals, insects — anything living and mobile.
Plants use あります despite being living things.
Vehicles do not take います even when a person is inside them (with some colloquial exceptions).

meaning: connecting form (basis for many compound constructions)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The て-form is one of the most important verb forms in Japanese. It does not express a tense by itself but serves as the foundation for many other grammatical constructions: requests (-てください), progressive aspect (-ています), permission (-てもいい), prohibition (-てはいけない), sequence of actions, and many more. Mastering te-form conjugation is essential because it unlocks a large portion of Japanese grammar.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Ichidan: drop る, add て (食べる → 食べて). Godan: depends on ending — う/つ/る → って; ぬ/ぶ/む → んで; く → いて; ぐ → いで; す → して. Irregular: する → して, くる → きて.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
行く is irregular: 行って (not いいて).
The て-form alone can also express a sequence: 朝起きて顔を洗う — 'get up in the morning and wash my face'.

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: -てください is the standard polite form for making a request. It attaches ください to the て-form of a verb. It is the default polite request form taught to beginners and is appropriate in most polite contexts, though it can sound slightly direct; softer variants (-ていただけませんか) appear later.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb-て + ください

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Negative request: -ないでください ('please don't')
Softer request forms (-ていただけませんか, -ていただけますか) are N4+ and more appropriate in very formal contexts.

meaning: be doing (progressive); be in the state of having done (resultant state)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: -ています has two related uses: (1) ongoing action — 'is doing' — analogous to English progressive; and (2) resultant state — 'has done and is now in that state' — particularly for change-of-state verbs like 結婚する ('get married'), 住む ('live'), 知る ('come to know'). In the second case, 結婚しています means 'is married' (not 'is marrying'). Distinguishing these two uses is an important step in early Japanese learning.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb-て + います

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
For action verbs (eat, read, walk), -ています expresses ongoing action.
For change-of-state verbs (get married, come to know, die), -ています expresses resultant state.
Plain form: -ている. Casual: often contracted to -てる.

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The ない-form is the plain-form negative of verbs, used in casual speech and as the basis for many grammatical constructions (-なければならない, -ないでください, -なくてもいい, etc.). It is the casual counterpart of ません.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Ichidan: drop る, add ない (食べる → 食べない). Godan: change the final う-row kana to the a-row, add ない (行く → 行かない, 話す → 話さない). Exception: ある → ない (suppletive, no あらない). Irregular: する → しない, くる → こない.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: casual

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
ある is suppletive: its negative is ない, not あらない.
Past negative: -なかった (食べなかった, 行かなかった).

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The た-form is the plain-form past tense of verbs. It shares its conjugation rules with the て-form, substituting た/だ for て/で. It is also the base for several compound constructions like -たことがある (experience) and -たほうがいい (advice).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Ichidan: drop る, add た (食べる → 食べた). Godan: same pattern as the て-form, with た/だ instead of て/で (行く → 行った, 話す → 話した, 飲む → 飲んだ). 行く is irregular: 行った. Irregular: する → した, くる → きた.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: casual

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Parallels the て-form in conjugation rules exactly.
Past negative plain: -なかった.

もう<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べた。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: い-adjectives end in い in the dictionary form and can stand as a complete predicate without any copula (高い — 'is high/expensive'). In polite speech, です is attached for politeness, but it is a politeness marker here rather than a true copula — compare 高いです, 高いでした (wrong), 高かったです (correct).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Stem + い (e.g., 高い, 新しい, 美味しい)

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Do not use だ or です as a copula with い-adjectives; です after an い-adjective is purely a politeness marker.
いい ('good') is irregular in past and negative forms — see i-adjective-negative and i-adjective-past.

sections.html: Drop い, add かった (plain) or かったです (polite). いい → よかった.

sections.html: な-adjectives behave grammatically like nouns: they use the copula (だ plain, です polite) to form predicates. The 'な' is only added when the adjective directly modifies a noun (static-adjective attributive form). Examples: 静か, 元気, きれい, 有名.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Common な-adjectives: 静か, 元気, 便利, 親切, 有名, きれい (note: きれい looks like an い-adjective but is actually な-adj), 嫌い (same).
Past, negative, and other forms use copula forms (see deshita, dewa-arimasen).

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
For actions, use -たい, not ほしい.
Third-person: use ほしがる or rephrase.
ほしくない (don't want), ほしかった (wanted), ほしくなかった (didn't want) — all regular い-adjective conjugations.

examples.jp: 新しい車がほしいです。
examples.furi: <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby>がほしいです。
お<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>がほしい。

examples.jp: 冷たい水がほしいです。
examples.furi: <ruby>冷<rt>つめ</rt></ruby>たい<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>がほしいです。

point: A のほうが B より + adjective

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The Japanese comparative construction uses のほうが on the more prominent item and より on the reference item. The order is flexible: both 'A のほうが B より' and 'B より A のほうが' are acceptable. The adjective describes the quality being compared.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: A のほうが B より + adjective (or B より A のほうが + adjective)

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
For nouns: use のほうが. For verbs: use the dictionary form + ほうが.
The construction is about direct comparison; for 'more X' without a specific comparison, use もっと.

examples.jp: 犬のほうが猫より大きいです。
examples.furi: <ruby>犬<rt>いぬ</rt></ruby>のほうが<ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>より<ruby>大<rt>おお</rt></ruby>きいです。

examples.jp: コーヒーよりお茶のほうが好きです。

examples.furi: <ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>のほうがバスより<ruby>速<rt>はや</rt></ruby>いです。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 一番 (いちばん) literally means 'number one' and is the standard superlative marker in Japanese. It precedes an adjective to express 'the most ___'. It is typically paired with で or の中で to specify the scope of the comparison ('among ___').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: (の中で) + 一番 + adjective

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Scope of comparison: 日本で一番高い山 ('the tallest mountain in Japan'), クラスの中で一番背が高い人 ('the tallest person in the class').
More formal alternative: 最も (もっとも).

examples.jp: 富士山は日本で一番高い山です。
examples.en: Mt. Fuji is the tallest mountain in Japan.

寿司が<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby><ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。

meaning: general-purpose counter for small things (one, two, three…)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The ～つ counter is a native Japanese counter used for most small objects, abstract items, and in cases where no more specific counter applies. It only goes from 1 to 10: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ, いつつ, むっつ, ななつ, やっつ, ここのつ, とお (10 is just とお without つ). Beyond 10, one uses a Sino-Japanese counter like 個 or an item-specific counter.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Japanese cardinal + つ (ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ…). For 10, use とお (just the number, no つ).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Only goes from 1 to 10. For 11+ use 個 (こ) or another specific counter.
Useful for age when counting young children: ふたつ = 2 years old, or more generally via 歳/才 counter.
Cannot be used for people or animals — those have their own counters.

examples.jp: りんごを三つください。
examples.furi: りんごを<ruby>三<rt>みっ</rt></ruby>つください。
<ruby>質問<rt>しつもん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>一<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>つあります。

examples.jp: 部屋に窓が二つあります。
examples.en: There are two windows in the room.
examples.furi: <ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>に<ruby>窓<rt>まど</rt></ruby>が<ruby>二<rt>ふた</rt></ruby>つあります。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: ～人 is the counter for people. It uses Sino-Japanese numbers from 3 onward (三人, 四人, 五人…) but 1 and 2 are irregular: ひとり (一人) and ふたり (二人). 4 is よにん (not しにん, which sounds like 'dead person'). This is one of the first counters learners encounter.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Sino-Japanese number + 人 (にん). Exceptions: 一人 = ひとり, 二人 = ふたり, 四人 = よにん.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
一人 and 二人 use native numbers: ひとり, ふたり.
四人 is よにん, not しにん (しにん = 死人 'dead person').
七人 can be しちにん or ななにん, both acceptable.

examples.en: There are four people in my family.
examples.furi: <ruby>家族<rt>かぞく</rt></ruby>は四人です。
<ruby>二人<rt>ふたり</rt></ruby>で<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。

examples.jp: パーティーに十人来ました。
examples.en: Ten people came to the party.
examples.furi: パーティーに十人来ました。

point: 何 / 誰 / どこ / いつ / どう / どうして
meaning: basic interrogatives: what / who / where / when / how / why

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The essential Japanese question words are 何 (なに/なん — 'what'), 誰 (だれ — 'who'), どこ ('where'), いつ ('when'), どう ('how'), and どうして or なぜ ('why'). 何 changes between なに and なん depending on the following sound: before t, d, n, or the copula だ/です, it reads as なん (何ですか = なんですか); elsewhere, なに. These question words are typically followed by が, は, or no particle depending on the sentence structure.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Place the question word where the unknown information would go in the answer. End with か in polite speech.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
何 reads as なん before t/d/n/desu sounds: 何ですか (なんですか), 何時 (なんじ), 何人 (なんにん). Elsewhere なに: 何を食べますか.
In casual speech, drop the か and use rising intonation.

examples.furi: これは<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby>ですか。
<ruby>誰<rt>だれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>来<rt>らい</rt></ruby>ましたか。
トイレはどこですか。

examples.jp: いつ日本に来ましたか。
examples.en: When did you come to Japan?
examples.furi: いつ<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>らい</rt></ruby>ましたか。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: ないでください is the negative counterpart of てください. It attaches でください to the ない-form of a verb and expresses 'please do not do X'.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb-ない + でください (drop nothing from the ない-form; just append でください)

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Note the form: 食べないでください, not 食べなくてください.
The particle で here comes from the て-form of the auxiliary ない (via ないで), not from the particle で.

examples.jp: ここで写真を撮らないでください。
examples.en: Please do not take photos here.
examples.furi: ここで<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>撮<rt>と</rt></ruby>らないでください。

examples.jp: 心配しないでください。
examples.furi: <ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>しないでください。

examples.jp: ここで食べないでください。
examples.furi: ここで<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べないでください。

meaning: X and Y (and so on) — non-exhaustive listing

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: や lists items non-exhaustively — 'X, Y, and so on' — implying there are other things not listed. It is often reinforced by など at the end. It contrasts with と, which lists items exhaustively.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + や + Noun (+ など)

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Use と for exhaustive listing ('X and Y, nothing else').
Use や for representative listing ('X, Y, and other things').

examples.jp: スーパーで野菜や果物などを買いました。
examples.en: I bought vegetables, fruit, and so on at the supermarket.
examples.furi: スーパーで<ruby>野菜<rt>やさい</rt></ruby>や<ruby>果物<rt>くだもの</rt></ruby>などを<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>いました。

examples.jp: 部屋に机やベッドがあります。
examples.en: There are a desk, a bed, and other things in the room.
examples.furi: <ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>に<ruby>机<rt>つくえ</rt></ruby>やベッドがあります。

examples.en: There are dogs, cats, and so on.
examples.furi: <ruby>犬<rt>いぬ</rt></ruby>や<ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>がいます。

meaning: won't you...? / would you like to...? (invitation)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜ませんか is formed on the polite negative verb ending ません plus the question particle か. Despite its literal 'won't you' shape, it functions as a polite invitation: 'would you like to do X with me?'. Contrast with 〜ましょうか, which is slightly more assertive ('shall we?'). Responses are typically はい or 〜ましょう for acceptance and a polite circumlocution for decline.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb ます-stem + ませんか (the same stem used for the ます form).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Functionally an invitation, not a literal yes/no question despite the negative shape.
Compare with 〜ましょうか (shall we) — ましょうか assumes the other party is amenable, while ませんか leaves more room to decline.
Often paired with 一緒に for 'shall we do X together'.

examples.jp: 一緒に映画を見ませんか。
examples.en: Would you like to watch a movie together?
examples.furi: <ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ませんか。

examples.jp: 明日、一緒に食事しませんか。
examples.en: Would you like to have a meal together tomorrow?
examples.furi: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、<ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>食事<rt>しょくじ</rt></ruby>しませんか。

examples.en: Shall we go to the park?
examples.furi: <ruby>公園<rt>こうえん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きませんか。

point: もう + Verb-た / ました

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: もう as an adverb of time means 'already' when used with past-tense verbs. The construction expresses that an action has been completed before some reference point. Its conceptual counterpart is まだ ('still / not yet'), which for 'not yet' uses the progressive negative rather than the simple past negative.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: もう + V た (plain past) or V ました (polite past).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
For the opposite 'not yet', use まだ + V ていない (NOT まだ + V ませんでした).
For 'already + state/continuous', use もう + V ている (もうわかっている 'I already understand').
もう can also mean 'any more' with negative future (もう行かない 'I'm not going any more') — a distinct use.

examples.furi: もう<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>をしました。

examples.jp: もうご飯を食べました。
examples.furi: もうご<ruby>飯<rt>めし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べました。
もう<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みましたか。

related: まだ + Verb-ていない / まだ + Verb-ている

point: まだ + Verb-ていない / まだ + Verb-ている

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: まだ has two related uses as a temporal adverb: (1) 'not yet' — paired with the progressive negative Vていない, expressing that an action has not been completed; (2) 'still' — paired with the progressive affirmative Vている, expressing that an action/state is ongoing. Crucially, 'not yet' uses the progressive negative, NOT the simple past negative — まだ食べていません, not まだ食べませんでした.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Not yet: まだ + V ていない / まだ + V ていません. Still: まだ + V ている / まだ + V ています.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
'Not yet' uses the progressive negative — a common error point for English speakers who reach for the simple past negative instead.
'Still' uses the progressive affirmative.
Distinguished from その他の まだ usages like まだ + adjective ('still X') or まだ + noun ('still a N').

examples.jp: まだ宿題をしていません。
examples.en: I haven't done my homework yet.
examples.furi: まだ<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>をしていません。
まだ<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べていません。

examples.en: My little brother is still sleeping.
examples.furi: <ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>はまだ<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ています。

point: V plain / i-adj / na-adj な / noun の + とき(に)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: とき creates a temporal 'when' clause that modifies a main-clause predicate. The に is optional and adds mild emphasis on timing. The verb in the とき clause can be present or past, which determines the temporal relationship to the main clause: V plain non-past + とき = 'when I do / am about to do X', V plain past + とき = 'when I did / was doing X'.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V plain (non-past or past) + とき(に); i-adj + とき(に); na-adj + な + とき(に); noun + の + とき(に).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Non-past V + とき: action happens at the time of / as X begins.
Past V + とき: action happens after X has occurred / during an ongoing X.
The connector particle matters: な for na-adjectives, の for nouns.
Can be written 時 or とき; both are common.

examples.jp: 子供のとき、よく公園で遊びました。
examples.en: When I was a child, I often played in the park.
examples.furi: <ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>のとき、よく<ruby>公園<rt>こうえん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>びました。

examples.jp: 日本へ行ったとき、友達に会いました。
examples.en: When I went to Japan, I met a friend.
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>ぎょう</rt></ruby>ったとき、<ruby>友達<rt>ともだち</rt></ruby>に<ruby>会<rt>かい</rt></ruby>いました。

examples.jp: 暇なとき、本を読みます。
examples.en: When I'm free, I read books.
examples.furi: <ruby>暇<rt>ひま</rt></ruby>なとき、<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みます。

related: V 〜ている / noun-の / adj + 間 or 間に

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜と一緒に expresses doing an action together with someone or something. The と particle marks the accompaniment partner; 一緒に is an adverb literally meaning 'together'. The full pattern 〜と一緒に is very common and is one of the standard ways to express 'with' in the sense of accompaniment. 一緒に can also stand alone without a partner (一緒に行きましょう 'let's go together').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + と + 一緒に + main-clause verb.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
と marks the accompaniment partner; 一緒に is the adverbial 'together'.
Can also appear without と when the partner is contextually clear: 一緒に行きましょう.
Different from と alone (as comitative): 〜と一緒に is slightly more explicit and emphatic.

examples.jp: 友達と一緒に映画を見ました。
examples.en: I watched a movie together with a friend.
examples.furi: <ruby>友達<rt>ともだち</rt></ruby>と<ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ました。

examples.jp: 家族と一緒に日本へ行きたい。
examples.en: I want to go to Japan together with my family.
examples.furi: <ruby>家族<rt>かぞく</rt></ruby>と<ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい。

examples.jp: 一緒に食事しませんか。
examples.furi: <ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>食事<rt>しょくじ</rt></ruby>しませんか。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: だけ is the neutral restrictor meaning 'only' or 'just' — expressing that nothing else is included. It attaches to nouns, numbers, or counters. Contrast with ばかり (N3), which adds an emphatic 'nothing but' nuance often with implied criticism. だけ is the more neutral, register-appropriate choice for basic restriction.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + だけ; Number/counter + だけ (一つだけ 'just one'). Can follow or replace case particles.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Neutral register — contrast with ばかり which is emphatic/critical.
With numbers or counters, expresses 'just X much': 一人だけ ('just one person'), 少しだけ ('just a little').
Can combine with で to say 'just with X': これだけで ('just with this').

examples.furi: <ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>だけ<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みました。
<ruby>一人<rt>ひとり</rt></ruby>だけ<ruby>来<rt>らい</rt></ruby>ました。
これだけでいいです。

related: Noun / verb (〜て form / plain) + ばかり

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The 〜く form of an i-adjective is its adverbial form — used to modify a verb or another predicate ('do X -ly'). It is the same stem used as the base for negative (〜くない) and past (〜かった) forms, so it is a foundational component of i-adjective conjugation. The irregular exception is いい → よく.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Drop final い from the i-adjective, add く: 早い → 早く, 大きい → 大きく, 高い → 高く. Irregular: いい → よく.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Exception: いい conjugates as よい throughout its stem-based forms — よく, よくない, よかった.
The same 〜く form is the stem for negatives (〜くない) and past (〜かった).
Parallel to the 〜に form for na-adjectives.
Commonly used with verbs of action or change: 早く起きる ('wake up early'), 大きく書く ('write big').

examples.furi: <ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きてください。

examples.jp: 大きく書いてください。
examples.furi: <ruby>大<rt>おお</rt></ruby>きく<ruby>書<rt>しょ</rt></ruby>いてください。
よく<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>します。

related: い-adjective stem + くない / くありません

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The 〜に form of a na-adjective is its adverbial form — used to modify a verb ('do X in an X manner'). Parallel to the 〜く form for i-adjectives. The full phrase 〜にする ('make X so') is a productive construction built on this adverbial form (静かにする 'make quiet / be quiet'; 元気にする 'make/keep energetic').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: na-adj root + に: 静か → 静かに, 上手 → 上手に, 元気 → 元気に, きれい → きれいに.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Parallel to i-adj 〜く but with a different final particle (に vs く).
No conjugation: the に form is adverbial and stable.
The productive compound 〜にする ('make/keep it X') is used across many na-adjectives.
Pair with a verb for adverbial modification: 静かに歩く ('walk quietly').

examples.furi: <ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かにしてください。

examples.jp: 日本語を上手に話します。
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語を<ruby>上手<rt>じょうず</rt></ruby>に<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>します。
<ruby>元気<rt>げんき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>歌<rt>うた</rt></ruby>いました。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜くて is the 'te-form' of i-adjectives, used to join clauses. It functions like the verb te-form: linking adjective phrases together ('X and Y') or giving a reason/cause ('X, so Y'). It is distinct from the 〜で form used for na-adjectives and nouns. Exception: いい → よくて.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Drop final い, add くて: 高い → 高くて, おいしい → おいしくて, 寒い → 寒くて. Irregular: いい → よくて.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Cannot use で for i-adjectives — that is reserved for na-adj and nouns.
Exception: いい → よくて (matching the よく / よかった pattern).
Can chain multiple adjectives: 高くて、重くて、使いにくい ('expensive, heavy, and hard to use').
Causal usage: 寒くて、外に出たくない ('it's cold, so I don't want to go out').

examples.en: This book is expensive and heavy.
examples.furi: この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>高<rt>だか</rt></ruby>くて、<ruby>重<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い。

examples.jp: 彼女は優しくて、きれいです。
examples.furi: <ruby>彼女<rt>かのじょ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>優<rt>やさ</rt></ruby>しくて、きれいです。

examples.jp: 寒くて、外に出たくない。
examples.en: It's cold, so I don't want to go outside.
examples.furi: <ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>くて、<ruby>外<rt>そと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たくない。

meaning: te-form of na-adjectives and nouns (joining / causal)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The 〜で form is the copular 'te-form' used for na-adjectives and nouns. It joins clauses just like 〜くて for i-adjectives: 'X and Y' or 'X, so Y'. The same で form works for both na-adjectives and noun predicates, reflecting the underlying shared copula だ.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: na-adj root + で: 静か → 静かで, 元気 → 元気で. Noun + で: 学生 → 学生で, 会社員 → 会社員で.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Parallel to 〜くて for i-adjectives but with a different particle (で instead of くて).
Same で form for na-adjectives and nouns, reflecting the shared copula.
Can chain: 静かで、きれいで、広い ('quiet, clean, and spacious').
Causal usage: 彼は医者で、とても忙しい ('he is a doctor, so he's very busy').

examples.jp: この部屋は静かで、きれいです。
examples.en: This room is quiet and clean.

meaning: both X and Y / neither X nor Y

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜も〜も pairs two nouns with the particle も to express 'both X and Y' (with affirmative predicate) or 'neither X nor Y' (with negative predicate). The polarity flips depending on the main clause's predicate. Common for inclusive listings.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + も + Noun + も + (affirmative for 'both' / negative for 'neither').

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Affirmative main clause: 'both X and Y' — コーヒーも紅茶も好きです ('I like both coffee and tea').
Negative main clause: 'neither X nor Y' — コーヒーも紅茶も飲みません ('I drink neither coffee nor tea').
The same pattern extends to three or more items.
Distinct from separate も markers — the two-item pair forms a coordinated construction.

meaning: X and Y (exhaustive listing of nouns)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The particle と between nouns forms an exhaustive list — 'X and Y (and nothing else)'. Distinct from や, which is non-exhaustive ('X, Y, and others'). と is the go-to particle for complete enumerations of a set of items. Each pair or triple of items is connected with と between adjacent items.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + と + Noun (+ と + Noun ...).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Exhaustive: the listed items are the complete set — no others implied.
Contrast with や (non-exhaustive): 本と鉛筆 ('a book and a pencil, exactly these two') vs 本や鉛筆 ('books, pencils, and other things').
Only connects nouns — not verbs or adjectives.
Can chain: りんごとバナナとみかん ('an apple, a banana, and an orange').

meaning: location relative to a reference (above, below, inside, in front, behind, next to)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: Japanese uses location nouns (位置名詞) to describe spatial relations: 上 (above), 下 (below), 中 (inside), 前 (in front of / before), 後ろ (behind), 横 (beside), 隣 (next to, same type), 間 (between). The pattern is [reference noun] の [location noun] + particle. The に particle marks the location for existence verbs (あります/います); で marks the location for action verbs.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Reference noun + の + location noun + に/で/へ + verb.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Common location nouns: 上, 下, 中, 前, 後ろ, 横, 隣, 間, 右, 左, 外, 近く.
の is required between the reference noun and the location noun.
に for existence/static location; で for action verbs; へ/に for direction.
隣 implies the adjacent item is the same type (隣の家 'the next house'); 横 is more general 'beside'.

For asking age politely: おいくつですか.

For asking clock times and meeting times.

meaning: what day of the week / days of the week

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 何曜日 (なんようび) asks 'what day of the week'. The days of the week follow the 曜日 pattern: 月曜日 (Monday), 火曜日 (Tuesday), 水曜日 (Wednesday), 木曜日 (Thursday), 金曜日 (Friday), 土曜日 (Saturday), 日曜日 (Sunday). Named after the sun (日), moon (月), and the five classical elements: fire (火), water (水), wood (木), metal (金), earth (土).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Question: 何曜日. Each day: [element kanji] + 曜日. Time marker: 〜曜日 + に ('on [day]').

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Each day named after a celestial body or classical element.
Pattern: 月/火/水/木/金/土/日 + 曜日.
With particle に for 'on [day]': 月曜日に ('on Monday').
Short form 〜曜 (without the 日) is used in casual schedules.

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜時 (じ) is the counter for clock hours — 'X o'clock'. Numbers 1-12 are used, but several have irregular readings: 4時 (よじ), 7時 (しちじ), 9時 (くじ). Combined with 〜分 (minutes) for specific times. Used with particle に for 'at X o'clock'.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Number + 時. Irregulars: 4 → よ, 7 → しち, 9 → く.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Irregular readings: 4時 (よじ, NOT しじ), 7時 (しちじ), 9時 (くじ, NOT きゅうじ).
Paired with 分 for precise times: 3時15分 (さんじじゅうごふん).
With particle に for scheduled time: 9時に (at 9 o'clock).

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜分 (ふん / ぷん) is the counter for minutes — both clock-time minutes and duration. Reading changes between ふん (voiceless) and ぷん (voiced / geminated) depending on the preceding number. Several numbers have irregular or combined forms. Common contexts: clock time (3時10分), duration (10分), distance by time (駅から5分).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Number + 分. Reading: ぷん after 1/3/4/6/8/10; ふん after 2/5/7/9. Half-hour fixed form: 半 (はん, for 30 minutes).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Reading rules: 1ぷん, 2ふん, 3ぷん, 4ぷん, 5ふん, 6ぷん, 7ふん, 8ぷん, 9ふん, 10ぷん.
Half-hour 30 minutes is often written as 半: 3時半 ('3:30').
Used for both clock minutes and duration.
Same kanji 分 has other readings (ぶん for 'share') and meanings.

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜歳 (さい) is the counter for age — the number of years a person has lived. The alternate kanji 才 is commonly used, especially in casual writing. Several readings are irregular: 1歳 (いっさい), 8歳 (はっさい), 10歳 (じっさい / じゅっさい), and 20歳 (はたち, a fully irregular traditional reading for 20 years old).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Number + 歳 (or 才). Irregulars: 1→いっ, 8→はっ, 10→じっ/じゅっ, 20→はたち.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
20歳 has the fully irregular traditional reading はたち — especially important because it's the age of legal adulthood in Japan.
For casual asking: 何歳 (なんさい); polite: おいくつ.
Kanji variation: 歳 (formal) vs 才 (casual / abbreviated).

sections.html: 〜円 (えん) is the counter for Japanese yen — the national currency. Numbers attach directly without sound changes. Used for all prices, costs, and monetary amounts. Question form: いくらですか or 何円ですか.

No irregular readings — attaches cleanly to all numbers.
Questions: いくらですか (more common) or 何円ですか.
Larger amounts use 万 (10,000) and 億 (100,000,000): 10万円 ('100,000 yen').
Written in full kanji for formal contexts, numerals for casual.

sections.html: 〜本 (ほん / ぼん / ぽん) is the counter for long, thin objects — pencils, bottles, umbrellas, trees, bananas, wire, roads, trains, phone calls, films, etc. The reading changes between ほん (voiceless), ぼん (voiced), and ぽん (geminated) depending on the preceding number.
